title: Chunk entropy debug playbook — SSE backpressure scratch
content:
Purpose:
Quick working notebook for a recurring class of streaming failures observed in staging and a narrow production cohort: intermittent "chunk entropy" (my shorthand) where SSE frames either arrive with varying small sizes or stop altogether for 50–500ms, then surge. Suspect interaction between per-connection batching/aggregation and downstream drain/backpressure (nginx/proxy + runtime KV cache behavior).

Symptoms observed (examples):
- Client sees a sequence of very small events (1–32 bytes) for ~200ms, then a burst of larger events. UX: partial message flicker, duplicated partial lines in some clients (race in reassembly).
- On the server, p99 request token latency spikes during periods of bursty output.
- A subset of requests (usually long-form generation > 1k tokens) end with client-side "stream closed unexpectedly" or "unexpected EOF" after a long period of micro-chunks.
- tcpdump of one session shows many small TCP segments with in-order ACKs, followed by a gap and then a block of data. No retransmits in most cases.

Repro notes (local + staging):
- This is intermittent. Deterministic repro is hard, but can increase occurrence by:
  * forcing smaller write buffer sizes on server and introducing a slow reader on client
  * enabling aggressive batching in the runtime: set BATCH_WINDOW_MS=12 and BATCH_MAX_TOKENS=256
  * stress with multiple concurrent streams (20–60) on a single worker GPU instance

Minimal repro commands (staging):
1) curl SSE client (quick probe)\
   TOKEN=redwood-local-token
   curl -v -N \
     -H "Accept: text/event-stream" \
     -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
     -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
     -d '{"prompt":"<long prompt>", "max_tokens":1600, "stream":true}' \
     "https://staging.api.redwood.ai/v1/generate?model=redwood-1-3b"

   Notes: -v + -N to disable buffering. Look for repeated "event:" frames and timestamps. "Connection: keep-alive" should remain open, but you might see long quiet periods.

2) Python async client (httpx) to reproduce slow-consume behavior:
   import asyncio
   import httpx

   async def slow_consume():
       headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {TOKEN}", "Accept": "text/event-stream"}
       async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=None) as client:
           async with client.stream('POST', URL, headers=headers, json=payload) as r:
               async for chunk in r.aiter_bytes(chunk_size=8):
                   await asyncio.sleep(0.05)  # slow reader -> causes backpressure
                   print(len(chunk), chunk[:80])

   Observed: forcing the client to sleep during read increases the fraction of micro-chunks in subsequent bursts.

3) Local go client that prints frame boundaries and delays between them (for precise timing)
   - Observed timings: median inter-frame 8ms during normal flow; during incidents, we see sequence: 4ms, 5ms, 3ms, 250ms gap, then 1 payload of 1200 bytes.

Server-side capture commands: (use on staging worker node)
- tcpdump capture (filter by connection):
  sudo tcpdump -s 0 -w /tmp/stream-conn.pcap host 10.11.12.13 and port 443
- strace on runtime process (short runs only):
  sudo strace -f -p <worker-pid> -e write,sendto -s 200 -o /tmp/strace.log  # look for small write() syscalls close together
- run go-fd-snooper on unix socket between runtime and frontend to see per-write size

Error snippets collected: (raw copy-paste)
- client logs:
  EOF while reading response body (httpx._exceptions.ReadError: unexpected EOF)
  "stream closed" after 3.4s of micro-chunks

- runtime logs around same request:
  2026-01-15T10:12:41.203Z INFO stream: writing frame 0 size=24
  2026-01-15T10:12:41.208Z INFO stream: writing frame 1 size=16
  2026-01-15T10:12:41.212Z INFO stream: writing frame 2 size=12
  2026-01-15T10:12:41.460Z WARN stream: client slow-read detected, pause=248ms
  2026-01-15T10:12:41.712Z INFO stream: flushed aggregate size=1344

- nginx/proxy logs (no 5xx):
  upstream response time: 0.22 / 2.41 / 2.92 (varies)

Hypotheses (ranked):
1) Upstream write coalescing + client slow-read interaction: runtime emits many small writes (each token or small chunk), kernel coalesces into small TCP segments; if client socket buffer fills briefly, kernel signals backpressure and runtime stops writing, leading to the gap. When resumed, pending buffered data is flushed as a large packet.
2) Proxy (nginx) is performing some buffering/flush alignment (proxy_buffering on) that interacts poorly with our per-write flushing in the runtime. Some older nginx configs will buffer and only flush on newline or after buffer fill; combined with small writes this can produce the observed micro-chunk then gap pattern.
3) Our KV cache + prefix reuse: when cache yields hit/miss transitions mid-request, runtime switches code paths (fast path emits token-by-token, miss path does batched writes). Switching between these modes could create variable chunk sizes.
4) TCP-level delayed ACKs + Nagle interaction with many small writes. If the runtime sets TCP_NODELAY inconsistently across code paths, mixes of delayed ACKs and Nagle could cause micro-chunking then burst.

Quick checks to falsify hypotheses:
- Force proxy disable (bypass nginx) and run same client; if problem reduces, proxy is suspect.
- Toggle proxy_buffering off on a staging nginx and re-run: sudo sed to set proxy_buffering off for route -> reload nginx -> test.
- Ensure runtime sets TCP_NODELAY always: audit socket creation sites.
- Add explicit flush semantics in runtime: write \"data: <chunk>\\n\\n\\n\" + call fsync-style flush (or flush on http writer). If that reduces small writes, then kernel coalescing behavior is the main factor.

Instrumentation to add (short-term):
- Log per-connection write syscall sizes in runtime (aggregate sample) with timestamps (like strace but lightweight)
- Emit a per-request marker when we switch code paths (kv cache miss->hit, batch flush boundaries)
- Add a small telemetry tag on responses for observed micro-chunk ratio (numWrites < 64B / totalWrites) and include in SLO dashboards.

Known attempted mitigations and results:
- Added small 4ms intentional sleep between token writes in canary: micro-chunk count decreased (surprising) but end-to-end latency increased 8–12%. UX improved in slow clients but throughput dropped.
- Enabled proxy_buffering off in one staging host: incidence dropped ~60% for that host.
- Force consistent TCP_NODELAY in runtime sockets: inconclusive, sporadic reduction.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Is there a user-agent/client pattern that amplifies this (some clients may read bytes eagerly vs line-based)? We have some evidence that node-fetch + EventSource is more sensitive than curl. Need to collect client types from production incidents.
- Is the KV cache toggle happening mid-stream for long requests? Add telemetry to mark exact token index when code path toggles.
- Can we add a tiny write coalescer in runtime (batch token outputs at 8–16 token boundaries) as a configurable option for Dedicated customers? Measure latency/cost tradeoff.

Next actions (owner: Aisha unless reassigned):
- [ ] Add per-connection small-write telemetry (PR draft: https://github.com/redwood/repo/pull/2345). (Liam to review)
- [ ] Run A/B on staging: proxy_buffering off vs on for 24h, measure micro-chunk telemetry. (Sofia to run)
- [ ] Add explicit per-request code-path markers to logs (kv hit/miss). (Small change; low risk)
- [ ] Collect client UA breakdown for incidents from the last 30 days (Telemetry query: STREAM-827).

Notes to self: keep this lightweight. The goal is to capture breadcrumbs and a small reproducible harness so QA can exercise slow-read scenarios. Avoid changing global defaults until we understand latency tradeoffs.

Quick reference commands (one-liners):
- Capture conn pcap for pid mapping: sudo ss -tpn | grep <pod-ip> ; then tcpdump host <client-ip> and port 443 -w out.pcap
- Disable nginx proxy_buffering for route (staging): add "proxy_buffering off; proxy_max_temp_file_size 0;" to location block and nginx -s reload
- Run slow python client: python -c "import asyncio,httpx; ..." (see snippet above)

If you pick this up: ping me in #eng-runtime with STREAM-827 in the title. I'll attach annotated pcap and strace extracts.

Revision history:
- 2026-01-08 initial notes and local probes
- 2026-01-20 added runtime log excerpts and hypothesis list
- 2026-02-14 added staging A/B results and next-action checklist

End.
